subtype: Approach: seeking professional support [Action]

The waiting room at the town clinic smelled of phenyl and of marigolds from the small shrine by the desk. Nandini held a folded notebook page. On it, in order: "Can't sleep past 4. Crying in the office washroom. Dread before opening email. Three months." Her friend Ira had made her promise to bring the list instead of searching her symptoms online at midnight and scaring herself.
When her name was called, she read the list out instead of saying, "I'm fine, just tired." The doctor asked questions, checked a few things and suggested she also see the counsellor on the second floor. Nandini booked the first slot, Thursday at four, before leaving.
That night, instead of reading articles, she wrote down what the doctor had asked her to track until Thursday: sleep times and mood each evening. She texted Ira: "Done. Thursday next."

qa.a: Nandini booked the first slot, Thursday at four.

qa.q: Why did Nandini read the list out instead of saying she was fine?
qa.a: She was anxious and worn down, but she had promised Ira and felt it was safer to be honest than to play it down again.

qa.q: Why is Nandini's approach wiser than searching symptoms online at midnight?
qa.a: A doctor could ask questions and plan next steps with her, rather than her guessing and frightening herself; keeping the counsellor appointment is the sensible next step.

qa.a: Ira is probably relieved and glad Nandini followed through, having been worried enough to ask for a promise.

Dear Tanuja,
In March you told me I sounded "hollow" on our calls, and I laughed it off. I'm writing to say you were right, and that I've done something about it.
For weeks I'd been reading lists online at 2 am and deciding what was "wrong" with me. Every article gave a different answer and a new worry. Last Tuesday I stopped doing that and booked an appointment with the counsellor our office offers.
I nearly cancelled twice. In the session I just described it: no energy for anything, even at weekends, and a sinking feeling when my laptop starts up. The counsellor didn't give me a label. There were lots of questions, and we made a plan together: weekly sessions for now, and a visit to our family doctor as well. I've booked both.
It feels strange to plan getting better like a project. It also feels steadier.
Zeenat

qa.a: Tanuja said Zeenat sounded "hollow" on their calls.

subtype: Approach: root cause analysis of the work drivers [Thinking]

Uday sir pushed his reading glasses up and looked at Dilnaz's third cup of tea. "You look the way I did at twenty-five. Let me tell you what I did then.
I was so tired I fell asleep on the bus to the office. Everyone said, take rest. But one Sunday I sat with a notebook and wrote: why am I this tired? Then I kept asking why. Because I work till ten. Why? Because I finish Mohan's reports as well as mine. Why? Because I never say no. And why is everything urgent? Because my manager called five things 'top priority' and none of them were ranked. Then I counted: eleven months without a single day of leave.
Rest would have fixed one Sunday. Those answers told me what to change. On Monday I asked my manager to rank the five. I gave Mohan's reports back, politely. And I applied for leave that same week."

qa.q: How long had Uday gone without leave?
qa.a: Eleven months without a single day of leave.

qa.q: What was the young Uday feeling before that Sunday with the notebook?
qa.a: He was exhausted enough to fall asleep on the bus, and likely frustrated that everyone's advice to rest didn't touch the real problem.

qa.q: Which choice in Uday's story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Asking why again and again, because it turned vague tiredness into causes he could act on: ranking the priorities, returning Mohan's reports and taking leave.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt when the reports were handed back?
qa.a: Mohan may have felt surprised or a bit awkward at first, but it was done politely and made clear whose work was whose.

grounding: It shows a man asking why he is exhausted and finding unranked priorities, no leave for eleven months and other people's tasks, which lets him change more than just resting.

The 7.42 local was packed, and Ramesh had exactly twenty minutes before his station and one hand free. Jasleen's message from last night was still open: "Stop saying you need a holiday. Why are you tired? Actually list it."
Squashed against the door, he typed into his notes with a thumb.
Why tired? Up till 1 most nights.
Why? Finishing things for Arun and Priti's team, not mine.
Why do I take them? Nobody told me what's mine first. Three bosses, three "urgents".
Leave? He scrolled his calendar. Last day off: the previous August. Eleven months.
The train jolted and his phone nearly slipped. He read the list again. It wasn't that he was weak. There were three causes, and a holiday would fix only one. He sent it to Jasleen with one line: "Okay. Monday I ask which boss ranks first."

I had nineteen days of leave sitting unused, and I'd stopped being able to read a whole email without drifting. So in February I made a list and took it to Nirmala, my manager, instead of just sighing at my desk.
First: two weeks' leave from the 10th. Second: I'd hand over the vendor audit to Pooja and the training rollout to Imtiaz, with a handover note each, before going. Third, and this was the hard one to say aloud: when I came back, could I have a lighter month? Only my own project, and no new work until April.
Nirmala read it twice and said yes to all three. "Reena, I'd rather have you back slowly than not at all," she said. The handovers took two long days. The leave felt strange for the first four days, then good. Coming back to half a load was the part that actually helped.

Wednesday, 4 September. This time he writes just three lines on a card: in bed by 11. Twenty-minute walk after dinner. Phone in the kitchen drawer from 10. His neighbour Asif, who walks his dog at nine, says, "Come with us." Vijay does, a little embarrassed at how slow he is.
Friday, 27 September. The card is soft at the edges. He missed the walk twice when it rained and slept late once after a match. But most nights he is asleep before midnight, and on Tuesday he got through the afternoon meeting without his usual third coffee.

I'd come home from the bank at eight, eat standing up and watch cricket clips on my phone till two. Mornings, I dragged myself in. The walk was the easiest. The sleep time took a month. The screen-free hour, honestly, I still cheat on sometimes. But three small things I could keep. The big plan I couldn't."

Nitin, you remember when you told me, "Naveen bhai, you look like a ghost"? I laughed and said I just needed discipline. That was my whole theory: I was tired because I was soft.
So I set the alarm for 4.30 and started working two hours before office. I cut Sunday badminton. I stopped taking lunch breaks. For about ten days I felt heroic.
Then the mistakes started. I sent a client the wrong quotation, twice in one week. I forgot our own team review. In the afternoons I'd read the same line five times. My manager asked if something was wrong at home. Nothing was wrong at home. I had taken a tired body and given it less rest.
More effort didn't fix the tiredness, Nitin. It fed it.

Shankar has the desk opposite mine in the planning office. In June he started arriving before the cleaners, around 6.30, with a flask and a grim look. He told me, "I've just been lazy. More hours, that's the fix." He stopped coming on the evening chai walk, then stopped eating lunch away from his desk.
I don't know what was going on inside him. I only know what I saw. By July his reports had more mistakes, not fewer. Twice our manager sent them back with red circles. He yawned through the Monday review and snapped at the intern over a spreadsheet. One afternoon I found him staring at his screen with nothing typed. I asked if he wanted to walk. He said, "I can't stop now, I'm already behind."
— Deepika

Jyoti leaned on the counter of the Aizawl branch and told the new trainee: "Let me tell you about Lalremsiami. When she was about your age, maybe twenty-five, she was the best clerk here and the most tired. She worked most Saturdays too. One March she took a whole week in Goa. She came back sunburnt and laughing, with cashew sweets for everyone. I thought, good, she's fixed.
But nothing here had changed. Same double counter, same Saturday shifts, same manager piling on reports. Within about three weeks she was quiet again. By April she was forgetting lunch and rubbing her eyes at four o'clock. She said to me once, 'The holiday was lovely. But I came back to the same chair.'
That line stayed with me. The next year, when I became manager, I stopped the Saturday shifts."

Monday, week three. Full days now. When he feels that thick-headed tiredness creeping in before the long review, he takes a ten-minute walk first instead of ignoring it.

"Six years ago, when Jasleen and I were newly married, we couldn't understand where the money went. Both of us earning, and by the 25th, nothing left. passage:
On the first of every month, once the milkman's bill was paid, Shankar and Tanuja sat on the charpai in their rented rooms behind the sugar mill. Tanuja wrote five headings in the notebook kept in the steel cupboard: rent, ration, bus and petrol, savings, and "fun". His wages from the mill and her tailoring money went into the first four lines first, and whatever was left went to fun.
On 19 March the bus-and-petrol line was empty; his scooter had needed a new tyre. Shankar looked at the fun envelope, which still held money for the temple fair. "Do we move it?" he asked. They talked it over while the rice boiled and moved half. The fair would still happen, with fewer sweets.

Zeynep and Zanele had shared a flat in Johannesburg for a year before they admitted their money talks weren't working. So on 1 August they cleared the kitchen table and made a plan on a big sheet of paper: rent, transport, groceries, savings, and one line Zanele insisted on calling "joy". Each line got an amount, and each of them paid a share in on payday.
It held until the 22nd, when the groceries line ran dry because Zeynep's cousin had stayed for a week. Zeynep offered to cover it herself. Zanele shook her head. "We're a team on this. Let's decide now, together." They moved some of the joy line to groceries, skipped the concert and cooked a big pot of lentil soup instead.
On 1 September they raised groceries a little and wrote "guests?" beside it.

qa.q: What did Zanele insist on calling the extra line?
qa.a: Zanele insisted on calling it "joy".

qa.q: Why did Zeynep offer to cover the groceries herself?
qa.a: Zeynep felt guilty and a bit embarrassed, since the cousin's stay had emptied the shared groceries line.

qa.q: What else could the flatmates try if a line keeps running out?
qa.a: At each monthly review they could look at the pattern and plan ahead for things like guests, as the note "guests?" begins to do.

qa.q: How does Zanele see the empty groceries line?
qa.a: Zanele treats it as a shared problem rather than Zeynep's fault, so deciding together feels fairer than one person paying.

grounding: It shows two flatmates setting category amounts, reviewing monthly and deciding together to move money from one line when another runs out.
